bullets: Classical: core actor sovereign nation-states; space as physical geography and static destiny; focus on military containment, territorial expansion, raw materials.
Critical: core actors political elites and media; space is a subjective, discursively built representation; focus on deconstructing dominant narratives and maps.
Feminist: core actors individuals and communities; space as everyday lived sites and intimate borders; focus on human security and bottom-up agency.
Business: core actors multinational firms; space as commercial corridors and supply chains; focus on sovereignty risk, border changes and value chain capture.
Compare paradigms on three axes: who acts, how space is seen, what the strategic focus is.
examTip: Likely a comparison of paradigms by actor, view of space and focus. Common mistake: mixing up Critical (narratives) with Feminist (lived everyday sites).

bullets: Christine de Pizan (1364-1430): City of Ladies (1405); women's perceived inferiority comes from denied education, not nature.
Clara Zetkin (1857-1933): socialist feminist; tied women's rights to the fight against capitalism; organised the first International Women's Day (1911).
Emmeline Pankhurst (1858-1928): WSPU leader; hunger strikes, window smashing, mass demonstrations; 'Deeds, not words'; linked to the 1928 Representation of the People Act.
Simone de Beauvoir (1908-1986): The Second Sex (1949); gender as a social construct ('One is not born, but becomes, a woman').
Marguerite Yourcenar (1903-1987): first woman in the Academie francaise (1980); Memoirs of Hadrian.
Rosa Parks (1913-2005): Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955); intersection of race and gender.
examTip: Be ready to match each figure to their idea/work and date. Common mistake: swapping Zetkin (socialist) and Pankhurst (suffragette tactics).

bullets: J. Ann Tickner (b. 1937): Gender in International Relations (1992); IR is gendered; security at individual/community level; power as 'agency with', not 'domination over'.
Donna Haraway (b. 1944): Simians, Cyborgs, and Women (1991); situated knowledges, against the 'God trick'; cyborg feminism.
Jennifer Hyndman (b. 1964): Managing Displacement (2000); scalar shifts, the body as scale; humanitarian aid and displaced persons.
Deborah Dixon: Feminist Geopolitics: Material States (2015); gendered and racialised material earth; visualities that justify military intervention.
Virginie Mamadouh (b. 1963): linguistic geopolitics, gendered citizens, European supranational identity.
Cynthia Enloe (b. 1938): 'Where are the women?', feminist curiosity, 'the personal is international', militarization of the domestic.
examTip: Expect matching scholar to key concept/text. Common mistake: confusing Haraway (situated knowledge) with Hyndman (scalar shifts, displacement).

session: Beyond the Western Gaze: Non-Western Thinkers
bullets: Gayatri Spivak (b. 1942): 'Can the Subaltern Speak?'; subalternity; strategic essentialism (use of minority identities for political goals).
Qin Yaqing (b. 1953): relational ontology (guanxi); 'logic of relationality' vs Western 'logic of rationality'; China's rise via social networks.
Keiko Sakai (b. 1960): Japanese IR; Middle East narratives, post-conflict Iraq and identity politics; Global South agency.
Jing Zhang: gendered statecraft; masculinised narrative of the Chinese state and diplomacy; female diplomats.
Maria Tanyag (b. ~1987): feminist political economy; links reproductive health to global security; bodily autonomy; hypermasculinity and 'strongman' logics.
examTip: Likely: match thinker to concept. Common mistake: attributing relationality to Spivak or strategic essentialism to Qin.

bullets: The slides organise the field around five themes: gender, individual, minorities, high vs low politics, epistemology.
Gender: definition of gender, gender in politics, gender discrimination (Stabilo campaign 2018 as example).
'Where are the women?': Lise Meitner (Hahn got the 1944 Nobel; she was nominated many times), Katherine Johnson (33 years at NASA), Edith Wilson ('Secret President', 1915-1921).
Individual and minorities: personhood, e.g. Te Urewera forest (2014) and Whanganui River (2017) recognised as persons in New Zealand.
Key point: any space is a geopolitical space, not only states and borders.
Epistemology links to Haraway: knowledge is situated, not neutral.
examTip: Be able to explain each theme with one example from the slides. Common mistake: treating feminist geopolitics as only about women, not about individuals and minorities too.

session: High Politics vs Low Politics and Rescaling
bullets: High politics: matters vital to state survival (military strategy, security, weapons, intelligence, elite diplomacy); coded rational and masculine.
Low politics: domestic, social, economic affairs (welfare, healthcare, public education, human rights); coded emotional and feminine.
The binary is not neutral: it privileges hegemonic masculinity (force, control, separation) and makes women and marginalised communities invisible.
Enloe: 'the personal is political, and the personal is geopolitical'; trace power to the kitchen table, factory floor and community clinic.
State scale: macro lens (treaties, boundaries, interstate conflict), state as unified actor.
Human scale: micro lens (homes, clinics, migration corridors); power analysed through effects on human bodies.
examTip: Likely an essay-style contrast of high/low politics and state/human scale. Common mistake: saying low politics is unimportant instead of explaining that it is coded as peripheral.
